items.title: Three parts, always in this order
items.caption: Tap a part to read what it does. Word by word the sentence says "Past I go", which English says as "I went."

parts.note: It goes in front and stamps the whole sentence as already done. It is always first, and it never changes.
It says who did it, in the slot before the verb. Swap it for *ia* and the same sentence is about someone else.
It names the action and keeps the same shape whether the going is past, present or still to come.

items.title: Build every sentence in the two tables
items.caption: Two pronouns and four verbs give the eight sentences printed above. The particle stays first and the verb stays last; only the middle word moves.

items.title: Put the three parts in order
items.intro: Tap the words to build the Samoan for each English sentence. Two of the words on offer do not belong.

items.why: The particle *sā* comes first, *ia* says she did it, and the verb *tāʻele* comes last.
*ʻOu* is I, and *fāgota* by itself means go fishing.
*Ia* is the pronoun for someone else, and *alu* is go.

items.title: Which sentence says it?
items.intro: Read the English, then choose the Samoan sentence that says it.

prompts.why: *Ia* is he or she, and *fāgota* is go fishing.
When rain falls there is no one to name, so the middle slot stays empty: the particle and the verb make the whole sentence.
*ʻOu* says I did it, and *tāʻele* is bathe.

items.title: Only the tune changes
items.caption: The words and their order stay the same. An English yes or no question lifts the voice at the end; a Samoan one usually falls and stays low over the last two or three syllables.

states.label: Statement
states.note: A statement. The book never marks its tune.

states.label: Samoan question
states.note: The same three words. The voice falls and stays low at the end, which is what the arrow ↘ marks in this book.

states.label: English question
states.note: English runs the other way: its yes or no question lifts the voice at the end.
